entities.summary:
Wilhelm Caspar Ferdinand Freiherr von Dörnberg was a German army officer who served in the French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars.

Born in 1810 in Stuttgart, Kingdom of Württemberg, he joined the Prussian Army at the age of 20 and distinguished himself in the Battle of Jena (1806) and the Battle of Auerstedt (1806).

He became a colonel in 1835 and played a key role in the suppression of the German uprising of 1848.

Von Dörnberg died on March 19, 1850, in Paris, France, and was buried in the Père Lachaise Cemetery.

His legacy is marked by his contributions to the development of modern artillery, particularly the use of rifled cannons, which had a significant impact on the outcome of the Napoleonic Wars.

Von Dörnberg's work also influenced the development of the Prussian military, which became a model for other European armies.

In the years following his death, von Dörnberg's legacy was largely forgotten, but in recent years, historians have sought to revive his reputation as a key figure in the history of modern warfare.

The von Dörnberg Museum in Stuttgart, Germany, is dedicated to his life and work, and his influence can still be seen in the design of modern artillery and military strategy.

entities.summary:
Wilhelm Caspar Ferdinand Freiherr von Dörnberg was a German army officer who served in the French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars.

Born on April 14, 1768, in Schloss Hausen, a chivalric estate in what is now modern-day Germany, von Dörnberg was a scion of the prominent Dörnberg family, known for their military and aristocratic connections. His upbringing and education at the prestigious military academy in Dresden shaped his future as a military leader.

Von Dörnberg's military career spanned over three decades, with notable assignments in the Prussian Army and later in the French Army, where he distinguished himself in battles against Napoleon's forces. His most notable military achievement came during the Battle of Austerlitz in 1805, where he played a crucial role in the Prussian forces' defeat. Despite this, his reputation as a skilled military strategist and leader endured, earning him recognition from his peers and superiors.

Following his military service, von Dörnberg returned to his family's estate, where he devoted himself to writing and historical research. His extensive writings on military tactics and the Napoleonic Wars provide valuable insights into the strategic decisions made during that period. Through his work, von Dörnberg left a lasting legacy that continues to inspire military historians and strategists today.

Von Dörnberg's life serves as a testament to the enduring influence of the aristocratic class in shaping European history, particularly during the tumultuous 18th and 19th centuries. His story is one of duty, loyalty, and the unwavering pursuit of excellence, even in the face of defeat.

His memoirs, 'The Austerlitz Campaign,' contain a poignant reflection of the harsh realities of war: 'War is a cruel mistress, but it is also a teacher.'
